title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.

title: Half-Plate GLP-1 Menus for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A menu-engineering kit that converts an independent restaurant's existing dishes into protein-first half-plates priced at about 65-75% of the full plate, to capture GLP-1 households that eat out smaller but still eat out.
customer: Independent and regional restaurants (10-60 seats, $1-4M revenue) in metros with a high share of higher-income Gen X and Boomer diners, paying $499 setup plus $99-149/month.
problem: Circana estimates 23% of US households now include a GLP-1 user and that these users will account for about 35% of food and beverage sales by 2030. Those households cut traditional retail food and beverage purchases, especially high-carb, high-sugar, refrigerated and frozen items, and shift toward protein, fiber, fresh produce and restaurant spending, yet they still outspend non-users. Big chains are chasing this, but independents have no menu-engineering staff. If they simply shrink portions at the same price, GLP-1 customers feel ripped off. If they shrink and cut the price proportionally, margins collapse.
solution: For each restaurant, a done-for-you overlay: 4-6 existing dishes re-specified as half-plates with protein grams, plate-cost and margin tables, pricing at 65-75% of full price to protect gross margin per cover, a small-plate 'protein first' section, and a nausea-friendly option (low-fat, low-volume). Deliverables include a printable menu insert, a QR page, POS/online-ordering item entries (Toast, Square, Clover) and simple local marketing via medspas, GLP-1 telehealth clinics and pharmacies that hand out a 'restaurants near you that fit your plan' card. Protein numbers come from recipe-level calculations, not vague 'healthy' badges.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is at household scale (Circana, November 2025), and oral versions (Wegovy pill December 2025, Foundayo April 2026) plus cash prices as low as $149-$299/month on TrumpRx.gov are pulling in more users. Novo Nordisk is cutting list prices to $675/month in January 2027. Meanwhile restaurant spending is recovering, with independents beating national chains and Gen Z leading (BofA, August 2026), so independent owners are looking for a differentiator national brands cannot copy quickly.
revenue_model: $499 one-time setup, $99-149/month for menu updates, QR/landing page and local partnership marketing. Optional performance share (for example, $1 per redeemed 'plan card'). Later: bulk licensing to regional chains and food-service distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The obvious read is 'GLP-1 kills food demand'. The data says something different: users cut retail food but restaurant spending rises and total spend still exceeds non-users, so the demand shifts channel and portion size rather than disappearing. The winner is margin engineering (a half-plate that keeps dollars per cover), not a health-halo badge. Evidence: Circana (Nov 18, 2025) https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 and https://www.circana.com/insights-hub/glp-1s-consumer-behavior (23% of households, 35% by 2030, restaurants up, retail food down, users skew Gen X with income over $100K). Independents outperform chains: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/restaurants-and-discretionary-spending.html . Caveat: the Circana pages I could read did not give the size of the restaurant-spend lift, so validate it with a few owners' POS data.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Walk in on 20 independent restaurants with a one-page free audit of their own top 5 dishes (protein grams, half-plate cost and price). Convert 5-8 into paid setups. In parallel, sign 2-3 medspas or pharmacies to hand out the plan card and track redemptions to build a case study. Target: 5 paying restaurants and one measurable uplift story (covers or check average on half-plates) by day 30.

title: Jobs-per-Megawatt Factory Recruiting for Public Power
one_liner: Represent municipal electric utilities in recruiting manufacturers by packaging spare feeder capacity, in-hand transformers and industrial rates into a 'jobs per megawatt' pitch that data centers cannot match.
customer: Municipal and public-power utilities and city economic-development agencies (retainer of roughly $3-6k a month). Manufacturers pay a success fee later.
problem: Data centers are absorbing grid capacity, and transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak while nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B, so reshoring is happening as retrofits that need power upgrades, not as new shells. Interconnection at investor-owned utilities takes years, and site selectors rarely look at small public utilities.
solution: A 'Load-Readiness Dossier' per feeder or substation: available megawatts, transformer status and lead times, industrial rate schedules, demand-charge modeling and permitting path. Match it to manufacturers with announced expansions (tariff-motivated onshoring, USMCA re-routers, foundries and magnet or metal processors) and to site selectors. Add a shared transformer reserve pool for small municipal utilities and help negotiate long-term service commitments.
why_now: Data-center demand collided with the reshoring wave in 2026. Section 232 tiers reward US-melted metals and full-value duties are pushing firms to add domestic capacity, and the machinery tier's 15% relief runs through 2027. Utilities are being asked to make loads decisions faster than most can handle.
revenue_model: $3-6k a month retainer per utility, a success fee per megawatt or per signed customer (paid by the manufacturer or shared), and optional financing of pre-bought transformer inventory.
non_obvious_insight: A public utility's incentives are the reverse of an investor-owned utility's. A 5 MW machining plant with hundreds of jobs beats a 100 MW data center with a few dozen jobs for a city council and for spreading fixed costs, yet no one markets to these utilities. Transformer-in-hand is the strongest closing argument.
first_30_days: Select 10 public-power utilities in manufacturing states (Ohio, Indiana, Tennessee, Texas, the Carolinas) and build dossiers from public tariffs, EIA data and integrated resource plans. Pitch 3 economic-development agencies and sign two paid pilot retainers.

title: Integrity Desk for Grant Applications
one_liner: Cross-funder screening that catches AI-mass-produced applications, recycled proposals and forged partner letters before reviewers waste time.
customer: Community foundations, corporate giving programmes, state and regional economic-development agencies and accelerators, reached through grant-management platforms such as Submittable and Foundant.
problem: NIH capped principal investigators at six applications a year (effective 25 Sep 2025) after one applicant filed 40+ apparently AI-generated applications, and it says AI-developed proposals are not original work. Funders elsewhere see multiples of prior volume. Letters of support and partner commitments are the easiest thing to fabricate, and the same proposal is shopped to many funders.
solution: A plug-in and API for grant portals. It scores text reuse and AI boilerplate across applicants (including anonymised cross-funder fingerprints) and verifies claims and citations. It automatically calls back signatories of support letters for signed confirmation, checks entity registrations, tax status and beneficial owners, and keeps a shared duplicate-application registry across member funders.
why_now: LLMs drove the volume flood that prompted NIH's 2025 policy. Foundation staffing is thin, and federal and state scrutiny of grant fraud is rising.
revenue_model: $5-25k per cycle for foundations, $0.50-5 per application via portal partners, and registry membership for funders.
non_obvious_insight: This is the cURL lesson. When the cost of submission falls to zero, the reviewer's attention is the scarce resource. The winning move is not detecting AI text, which is unreliable, but verifying checkable third-party facts, like a partner's confirmation call, that AI cannot fake for free.
first_30_days: Run free pilot scans on last cycle's applications for three community foundations through regional grantmaker associations. Publish anonymised findings such as the share of applications with heavy text overlap. Pitch one grant-software vendor for a plug-in partnership.

title: Sensor-Priced Insurance for Recovery and Peptide Clinics
one_liner: A specialty insurance program that covers contrast-therapy studios, IV and peptide bars and sauna clubs at lower premiums when their sauna, cold-plunge and session logs are streamed as underwriting data.
customer: Independent and small-franchise recovery studios and med-spa or peptide clinics with 1-5 locations, paying $4-12k a year per location. Excess-and-surplus carriers and wholesalers are the capacity partners.
problem: Standard general-liability policies exclude or misclassify saunas, cold plunges, IV therapy and peptides. Carriers have no loss history, so operators buy expensive surplus-lines cover. The real exposures are burns, syncope, slip-and-fall, water-quality infections such as Legionella, and unlicensed practice. Franchise growth in recovery is outrunning the insurance market.
solution: Start as a program manager or agency and grow into an MGA with a fronting carrier and reinsurance. Studios install a roughly $60-250 sensor kit that logs plunge temperature and sanitizer levels, sauna temperature and duration, session counts, waiver and health-screen completion, and staff certifications. A sensor-verified studio earns up to a 25% credit. The program adds an incident-reporting protocol, risk-engineering checklists and, over time, a proprietary claims pool.
why_now: HHS moved most Category 2 peptides back toward compoundable status in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on July 23, 2026, so peptides are entering clinics and recovery bars without a malpractice rating. Reinsurance is softening, with Jefferies expecting declines through 2027, and record cat-bond and traditional capital means niche programs can find cheap capacity. Recovery studios are among the fastest-growing small-format wellness businesses.
revenue_model: Commission of 12-15%, an MGA fee of 5-8% of premium, and a profit commission. Sensors and software add $49 a month. 500 locations at $8k premium is $4M of premium and about $700k of revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters have no loss data on cold plunges and the operators are the only ones who can generate it. A sensor-verified studio is a better risk than a paper-verified one, so the data flywheel is the moat. This is one of the first classes where the insured object, a plunge tank or sauna, can report its own hygiene and temperature.
first_30_days: Partner with a retail broker or E&S wholesaler that has a fitness or spa book. Get indicative terms from two E&S carriers on a credit for sensor-verified operators. Recruit 10 design-partner studios through owner communities and sauna or plunge dealer lists, giving them free sensor kits in exchange for logs. Aim for firm quotes within 90 days, and confirm licensing needs with counsel before quoting anything.

title: Fiduciary Collection Executor for Heirs
one_liner: A service that inventories, appraises and sells inherited card, comic, toy and coin collections for estate lawyers and executors, with an audit trail built for fiduciary liability.
customer: Probate and estate attorneys, trust officers, professional fiduciaries and family executors, billed per estate.
problem: Collections built by boomers and Gen X now carry five- to seven-figure values after record card prices, but heirs have no idea what they hold. 'We buy collections' buyers lowball, and executors are liable if they sell below fair value. Large estates and donations also need qualified appraisals.
solution: Photo-inventory intake (on-site or shipped kit), visual identification and comps, graded-versus-raw triage, sign-off by a qualified appraiser, and sale through the best channel (auction house, game store, streaming seller) under a published fee schedule. The output is an estate-ready valuation report with full custody and sale documentation.
why_now: Card prices are at records ($16.5M for a PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator, $1.4M for a PSA 9). Visual AI has cut cataloging cost sharply. The wealth transfer is under way.
revenue_model: A flat inventory and appraisal fee ($500-3,000) plus a 10-15% sale commission. Referral relationships with law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the collector but the fiduciary, who carries legal liability. Liability aversion unlocks budget, and the moat is trust artifacts (documented process, appraisal compliance) that any dealer cannot offer because the dealer sits on the other side of the trade.
first_30_days: Give a talk to 15 probate attorneys and 5 fiduciaries in one metro titled 'What is in Grandpa's basement.' Offer a $299 rapid triage, partner with a certified appraiser, and close the first 5 estates.

title: Robot Bullies: Paid Adversarial Pedestrian Panels
one_liner: A vetted panel of paid 'difficult humans' who kick, block, crowd and confuse sidewalk robots and humanoids on a controlled test range, so robot makers find their failures before the public does.
customer: Sidewalk delivery robot operators, humanoid and AMR makers preparing EU conformity files and retail or warehouse pilots, city permit offices that want interaction evidence, and robot insurers. First buyers are the safety or field-ops leads at 20 to 50 mid-size robot companies.
problem: Robots fail on human behavior, not physics. In 2026 an Uber Eats delivery robot was kicked over in Philadelphia, and robots circled in confusion in Lincoln Park in September. Each robot costs about $2,500 to replace, and the backlash is turning into permit fights. Makers test with polite employees or dummies. Nobody sells honest, repeatable samples of teens, drunks, kids, dog-walkers and wheelchair users behaving badly around a machine.
solution: A rented lot or closed street block set up as a 'behavior range', with a library of scripted provocations (path blocking, tailgating, encirclement by six teens, camera covering, gentle-force shoves, darting child-sized mannequins, cane and wheelchair users, leashed dogs). Screened, consented, insured participants are paid per session. Cameras and force sensors record everything. The output is a report formatted for conformity files and city permit filings, plus a recurring regression-testing subscription. Later: an anonymized 'Chaos Index' that ranks robot models by how they hold up against human misbehavior.
why_now: Sidewalk robots are now numerous enough to cause visible backlash, with the Philadelphia kicking incidents and the Lincoln Park swarm video. The EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027. ISO 25785-1, the first safety standard for legged and actively balanced robots, is still a draft, so makers have nothing to test against. Humanoid pilots are starting in warehouses and stores.
revenue_model: Test days at $8k to $25k per protocol set. Annual regression-testing subscriptions from $120k. Rev share with certification bodies (TUV, UL) on referred test packages. Licensing of anonymized behavior data to simulation and model teams.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not test-track capacity. It is honest human misbehavior at scale, and no simulator or employee panel produces it. The moat is the clinical-trial-style infrastructure: consent forms, insurance, screening and a bench of reliable trouble-makers. Robot makers will pay more for a 16-year-old's creativity than for another simulator.
first_30_days: Rent a parking lot on weekends. Recruit 30 paid participants from campus job boards at about $30 per hour. Have a lawyer draft consent forms and buy $2M of general liability. Pitch one local sidewalk-robot operator or university warehouse-robot startup a $5k to $10k 'chaos day' with a written report. Publish a free 'Chaos Report' on the Philadelphia-style behaviors to generate inbound leads.

title: Weather-Indexed Revenue Cover for Outdoor Micro-Businesses
one_liner: Per-day parametric policies that pay out within an hour when rain, heat or smoke hits a vendor's venue, priced from the vendor's own sales history.
customer: Farmers-market vendors, food trucks, festival vendors, ice cream and shaved-ice stands, seasonal farm stands and outdoor fitness operators.
problem: A rain day or heat wave can erase a day's sales and cannot be insured through conventional policies. Margins are thin, and small owners (about 64% of nonemployers in trouble) fall back on personal funds.
solution: Micro-policies bought per market day or season. A fixed payout triggers when measured rainfall, temperature or air quality at the venue exceeds a threshold during the market window. Premium and payout are calibrated to each vendor's baseline sales from POS or bank data, and payment goes out over instant rails. Distribution goes through market associations and POS apps.
why_now: Instant payout rails, POS and bank APIs for baseline sales, cheap gridded weather data, and reinsurer interest in parametric small-business products make this feasible for a small MGA team.
revenue_model: MGA margin on premiums of about $6-15 per vendor-day, plus program fees from market associations.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is manageable when triggers are set per venue and per day, and the product is cash within an hour of the rain rather than indemnity after paperwork. Vendors will buy small daily coverage bundled into their booth fee.
first_30_days: Partner with one market association (about 100 vendors) and an MGA or fronting carrier. Structure a season-long pilot under a master policy and price it from vendors' POS history. Track claims and basis risk.

title: Moonlighting and IP Clearance for AI Experts
one_liner: A concierge that checks and files the employer-disclosure, IP-assignment and confidentiality paperwork professionals need before moonlighting as AI-training experts, and issues clean-provenance certificates that labs and vendors can rely on.
customer: Employed lawyers, bankers, doctors, consultants and engineers doing expert-data gigs pay $79-149 per clearance. Data vendors and lab legal or procurement teams pay for an annual B2B license.
problem: Millions of experts have signed up, many still employed at banks, law firms and hospitals with outside-activity approval rules (e.g. FINRA-registered staff), IP assignment and confidentiality duties. Some platforms even solicit prior work that former employers may own (HN Apr 2026). One trade-secret suit could freeze a vendor's programs, and workers risk termination or licence discipline.
solution: (1) A contract reader flags moonlighting, IP and confidentiality risk in the worker's agreement and handbook. (2) Templates for the employer disclosure or approval request. (3) A scanner for confidential markers in submitted work. (4) A 'clean-room certificate' per contributor. (5) An onboarding API vendors can require. A partner attorney covers the advice.
why_now: The Mercor breach and class actions have made vendor risk teams and lab counsel nervous. Reports of labs asking contractors for real past work samples raise provenance stakes. The scale of professionals moonlighting for AI companies is unprecedented.
revenue_model: Per-clearance fee for workers plus $50-250k annual vendor licences and per-contributor API fees.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer with money is the vendor's general counsel, not the worker, but the worker channel gives distribution and data. A database of moonlighting and IP policies for the top few thousand employers, built from worker submissions, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 moonlighting experts. Hand-build 50 employer-policy profiles (big banks, Big 4, large law firms, health systems). Run a manual $99 concierge clearance service. Pitch two mid-tier data vendors' compliance leads a paid pilot.

title: Verified-Real Dating Portraits Shot by Wedding Photographers
one_liner: A consumer brand that rents wedding photographers' dead winter months to shoot candid-directed dating and profile portraits, delivered with a signed 'real photo' certificate.
customer: Single adults aged 25-45 in the top 20 US metros paying $179-299 per session. Secondary channel: matchmakers and dating coaches buying sessions for their clients.
problem: Wedding photographers earn most of their income in a compressed May-October window and sit mostly idle from November to March, with skills and gear already paid for. Meanwhile dating profiles are flooded with AI-generated and heavily retouched photos, so users and matches increasingly distrust every photo. Existing options are cheap AI headshot apps (the very thing everyone distrusts), generic corporate headshot studios that make stiff LinkedIn photos, and a few dating-photo studios with model-y aesthetics. Nobody is selling authenticity as a verifiable, human-shot product.
solution: A productized 60-minute walk-and-talk shoot across three locations using wedding-style directing prompts ('walk toward me and tell me the worst first date you've had') that get natural laughter from stiff people in about 90 seconds. Delivery is 15 edited photos in 48 hours following a dating shot list (full-body, hobby, social proof, pet, non-selfie smile). Each set ships with a 'Real Photo Certificate': Content Credentials (C2PA) from supported cameras, a no-generative-AI editing policy, and a public verification page users can link in their bio. Supply comes from wedding photographers trained in a 90-minute module. The platform handles booking, payment, brand, marketing and QC and keeps 30-35%.
why_now: AI-generated profile photos are now common enough that dating apps have leaned on photo and face verification. Several major camera makers now ship Content Credentials support in newer bodies or firmware, so provenance is technically feasible for small studios. Wedding photographers are also under margin pressure as couples trim coverage hours and guest counts, so winter income is increasingly attractive. 2026 is the first year 'proof a human made this' has real consumer value.
revenue_model: $199-299 per session with a 30-35% platform take. Upsells include a $39 'profile audit' and a re-shoot at 6 months. B2B2C packages for matchmakers and dating coaches at $150 per client.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce skill isn't lighting, it's getting a stiff stranger to laugh convincingly on cue, which wedding photographers do 40 times a summer. The photographer's marginal cost in January is close to zero, so supply arrives almost free while every competitor pays full-time studio rents.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and recruit 6 wedding photographers who complain publicly about winter. Run 20 pilot shoots at a $99 launch price, sourced from local Instagram/Reddit dating communities, run clubs and singles events, and from 5 matchmakers and dating coaches. Ask each client for before/after match counts (self-reported) and permission to publish testimonials. Register a public verification page for each set. Charge full price from shoot 21 onward.

title: Third-Party Maintenance for Orphaned Robots
one_liner: Like third-party server maintenance for IT, a spares-and-support contract for robots whose makers failed, were acquired or stopped supporting them.
customer: 3PLs, retailers, hospitals and factories running AMRs, storage systems and delivery robots that are out of warranty or whose vendors are gone, plus lenders and bankruptcy trustees holding stranded assets.
problem: Robotics funding is concentrating (Skild $14B, Physical Intelligence $11B, Figure $39B) while the long tail starves. Agility is pivoting toward wheels, and Serve's roughly $1.3k revenue per robot signals shakeout. Buyers can be left with multimillion-dollar fleets without updates or parts.
solution: Buy stranded inventory and spares from failed vendors, arrange source-code escrow or reverse-engineer key consumables, and offer annual per-robot support contracts with SLAs. Also sell certified refurbished units.
why_now: The 2025-26 funding boom is producing its first wave of failures and consolidation, while Amazon (1M+ robots, building its own robot factory) and Symbotic ($2.25B 2025 revenue) centralize the market. The orphan pool is growing now.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per robot per year in support contracts, refurbished-unit sales, and escrow and trustee fees.
non_obvious_insight: In every hardware boom the durable second-derivative business is keeping the losers' machines running. Buyers pay to avoid stranded assets, and your spares moat grows with each vendor that fails.
first_30_days: Identify 3 wound-down or struggling robot vendors, get trustee quotes on inventory (often pennies on the dollar), and approach their 5 largest customers. Sign 2 support contracts and open a small depot near Memphis or the Inland Empire.

title: Fake-Citation Triage for Defendants Facing Pro Se Filings
one_liner: A same-day report showing which citations in an opposing pro se filing are fake, misquoted or overruled, formatted as a court-ready exhibit for a motion to strike or for sanctions.
customer: Repeat defendants that get flooded with self-represented suits: landlord and property-management litigation groups, employment-defense boutiques, university and hospital counsel, insurer claims-litigation units, debt servicers, city attorney offices and municipal risk pools. Paid by the litigation budget owner.
problem: Charlotin's database holds about 2,095 AI-hallucination cases as of 28 Sep 2026, and 1,208 (58%) involve pro se litigants versus 829 involving lawyers. Pro se filers are immune to bar discipline, sanctions ($1,750 to $23,222) are slow and rare, and the defendant pays $300-600/hour of associate time to hand-check dozens of cites. Every hallucination-checker on the market is pitched to the lawyer who erred.
solution: Drag-and-drop a PDF. The tool extracts citations (open-source eyecite plus CourtListener), resolves each one, and flags nonexistent cases, quotes that do not appear in the opinion, wrong court or year, and negative treatment. Output is a two-page 'Citation Defect Declaration' plus a draft paragraph for a motion to strike or a Rule 11-type motion. Phase two hooks into the e-service email inbox so every incoming filing is screened automatically.
why_now: The volume of fabricated-citation filings is now measured in the thousands and judges have seen enough to act on them. Open case-law data (CourtListener) is now good enough that OpenAI built Astra for Law on it (17 Sep 2026), so the verification corpus is cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: $49-149 per filing report self-serve, or $1,500-5,000/month flat for repeat defendants with inbox integration. Upsell is drafting of the sanctions or strike motion at a fixed fee.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer everyone targets (the erring lawyer) has a small budget and an embarrassment problem. The money and standing sit with the counterparty, who pays hourly to verify someone else's junk and is the only actor who can turn a bad cite into leverage (strike, fee-shifting, vexatious-litigant designation).
first_30_days: Build on eyecite and the CourtListener API, then benchmark accuracy on 100 known cases from the Charlotin database as ground truth. Cold-email 30 landlord-tenant and employment-defense firms and 10 municipal risk pools, offering 10 free reports in exchange for permission to attach a report to a filing. Charge $99 per report after that and aim for 3-5 recurring accounts.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.

title: Mobile Cobot Safety Validation Lab
one_liner: A van-based lab that measures collision forces and signs off robot and cobot cells against the 2025 ISO 10218 revisions.
customer: Cobot distributors, integrators and 10-200 person manufacturers deploying cells. EHS managers and insurers are the second buyers.
problem: North American robot orders are broadening into semiconductors, pharma and food, and cobots are 15.4% of units. The 2025 revisions of ISO 10218-1 and -2 (which absorbed the collaborative guidance of ISO/TS 15066) require documented risk assessment and validation. Few engineers can do it, and force-measurement gear costs tens of thousands of dollars. Distributors skip validation and the liability lands on the shop and its insurer.
solution: A van with a calibrated force and pressure measurement device, safety-scanner zone tester and stop-time tester. Technicians validate on site (contact-force mapping by body region, speed and separation checks) and deliver a signed report. Software stores and versions results for audits. Annual revalidation is a subscription.
why_now: Revised standards are in force, robot demand is broadening to small shops and new sectors, and mobile manipulators are coming into plants.
revenue_model: $2.5-6k per cell validation. White-label contracts with distributors. About $1.2k a year for revalidation. Referral fees from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The limiting step for small-shop robots is fear of liability, not price. A third-party validation stamp is what insurers and owners want, and distributors have the incentive to sell but not the independence or equipment to certify.
first_30_days: Rent or buy a used force-measurement device. Sign three cobot distributors. Complete a machinery functional-safety credential. Validate the first five cells at a discount.

title: Proof-of-Review Receipts for AI-Using Professionals
one_liner: A tamper-evident record that a named, licensed human actually reviewed AI output, backed by planted-error vigilance tests, sold to firms and their malpractice carriers.
customer: Mid-size law firms, accounting firms and physician groups using AI drafting or scribes, and the malpractice and E&O carriers, MGAs and brokers underwriting AI use.
problem: Courts worldwide have issued about 1,490 decisions on AI-hallucinated filings (1,000+ in the US by May 2026), with sanctions up to $110k and the first suspensions. More than 60% of carriers now ask about AI use in underwriting, and some add AI endorsements or exclusions. Firms cannot prove that attorney review happened beyond a policy memo.
solution: A review layer (Word and Outlook add-in, EHR plug-in, browser extension) that logs what the AI produced, what the human changed, dwell time, automated cite-check results and sign-off. It also seeds a random slice of reviews with canary errors (a fake citation, a wrong dose in a test document) to measure whether reviewers really catch them. A signed monthly review-integrity report goes to the carrier for premium credit or endorsement eligibility.
why_now: AI-hallucination sanctions are growing by about eight cases a day. The EPIC 2026 claims survey shows carriers seeing more AI-related claims, and carriers are rewriting applications and endorsements now.
revenue_model: $30-80 per professional per month, carrier and broker partnerships (revenue share on premium credits), and a cite-check add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The weak link is automation complacency, not just model hallucination. You can measure complacency the way airports measure screener vigilance, by planting known-bad items. Insurers will pay for measured human vigilance because it is a rating factor.
first_30_days: Partner with one legal-malpractice MGA or broker and 10 small firms (5-50 lawyers) through state-bar CLE channels. Ship a Word add-in that logs review and checks citations. Pilot canary errors with written consent.

title: Signed-Capture Verified UGC for DTC Ads
one_liner: A capture SDK and verification API that proves a testimonial video came from a real, purchasing customer, for brands exposed to the FTC's fake-review rules.
customer: DTC and e-commerce brands spending on paid social, UGC agencies and marketplaces, and performance-marketing agencies with legal exposure.
problem: The FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials (effective Oct 2024) covers AI-generated testimonials from people who do not exist, with civil penalties above $50k per violation. AI 'UGC ad' generators now produce fake customers, and creators can deliver them through marketplaces without the brand knowing. Brands want real customers for conversion and cannot tell the difference.
solution: A web and native capture flow that records a testimonial with device attestation (Apple App Attest, Play Integrity), a random liveness phrase and a signed C2PA manifest, linked to a verified purchase through a Shopify order token. It outputs a 'Verified Real Customer' badge and an evidence file per ad. A batch API scans videos delivered through other tools, attests what can be attested and flags what cannot.
why_now: The FTC rule is in force, platforms are labeling AI content, and avatar-UGC volume has exploded. Provenance signals in phones and the C2PA ecosystem make signed capture cheap.
revenue_model: $3-8 per verified video, $500-3k/month agency plans, and a Shopify app subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The authenticity premium is really a compliance premium. Liability sits with the brand rather than the avatar vendor, so a legal-risk budget pays for it, not a marketing budget.
first_30_days: Ship a web capture flow linked to Shopify order tokens before any native SDK. Recruit 10 DTC brands through Shopify communities and UGC agencies at $5 per video, and run one campaign comparing verified and unverified creatives.

title: Renewal-Match Agent for Concession-Market Renters
one_liner: An agent that tracks true net-effective rents nearby, negotiates a renewal match with the landlord's leasing bot, and moves you if they refuse, paid only on savings.
customer: Renters in concession-heavy markets (Austin, Atlanta, Dallas, Phoenix, Florida) on 12-month leases, with destination landlords paying locator fees on moves.
problem: New tenants get free months while renewing tenants often receive above-market quotes, a loyalty tax. Concessions hit 15.8% of stabilized units (Austin 37%), and renters cannot see net-effective rent or spare the time to shop.
solution: With permission, the agent monitors net-effective prices in comparable buildings via listings and leasing-agent chats. About 100 days before renewal it sends a 'match or we move' letter with evidence and negotiates with the landlord's AI. If declined, it books tours, handles the move and collects the locator fee from the new building.
why_now: Operators now deploy AI leasing agents that can answer instantly, and agent protocols (like MCP-style interfaces) are appearing in property platforms. At 34 days to lease, landlords want to avoid turnover.
revenue_model: 25% of first-year renewal savings, locator commission from destination landlords on moves (often 50-100% of a month's rent in Texas and Georgia), and a premium lease-vault tier.
non_obvious_insight: Rental pricing has the same new-customer-discount, loyal-customer-premium structure that made insurers and telcos vulnerable to automated switching. When both sides run machines, the price reflects true clearing rather than inertia.
first_30_days: Run a manual concierge for 50 Austin renters recruited from local subreddits and apartment groups, taking 25% of savings. Log every quote and outcome and publish an 'Austin loyalty tax index' to attract more.

title: 30-Day Capacity-Window Plan After Early Alzheimer's Diagnosis
one_liner: A productized sprint that uses the legally competent window after an early blood-test diagnosis to lock down legal, financial, safety and care plans.
customer: Newly diagnosed patients and their spouses or adult children, reached through memory clinics, neurology and primary-care practices, blood-test labs and elder-law firms. Employers with caregiver benefits are a secondary buyer.
problem: Blood tests cleared in 2025 mean many people learn they're on the path to dementia while still competent, with a 3-7 year window to sign POAs, choose agents, set financial guardrails, plan driving and firearm safety, decide on Leqembi and record wishes. After capacity is lost, it becomes a court fight. CMS GUIDE closed enrollment after one 2024 window, so nobody owns the first 30 days.
solution: A fixed-fee, nurse-navigator-led sprint: a capacity-timed legal package via partner attorneys (POAs, directives, HIPAA releases, updated will or trust), financial guardrails (bill-pay automation, bank trusted-contact, scam locks), a safety plan (driving, firearms, stove, wandering), a care roadmap with cost projections and a Leqembi decision aid, and 90 days of dyad coaching.
why_now: FDA cleared Lumipulse pTau217 in May 2025 and a second primary-care blood test in Oct 2025. Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M and it now has an at-home subcutaneous starting dose. Diagnosis is decentralizing while post-diagnosis coordination is not.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,500 fixed family fee, plus employer or LTC-insurer contracts. No referral payments from providers, to stay clear of anti-kickback issues.
non_obvious_insight: Earlier diagnosis is a legal-capacity clock, not just a medical event. The valuable window is the one when the patient can still sign, and every document signed in it prevents a $5-15k guardianship later.
first_30_days: Partner with two memory clinics and three elder-law firms, and deliver five pilot sprints at $1,500 each. Track documents executed while competent and family satisfaction.

title: ARIA Watch: Aide Eyes for Alzheimer's Drug Clinics
one_liner: A 60-second daily safety check done by the home aide or family for patients on anti-amyloid drugs, flagging the subtle change that precedes brain-swelling side effects, sold to the memory clinic that prescribes them.
customer: Neurology and memory practices and infusion or injection programs running Leqembi and Kisunla. The buyer is the practice manager or program nurse coordinator. The revenue partner is the patient's home care agency.
problem: Anti-amyloid drugs carry ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding) risk, mostly caught by MRI at scheduled points. Symptoms such as headache, dizziness, vision change, new confusion or seizures often appear between scans. A person with dementia cannot report them. The infusion nurse sees the patient for two hours every two weeks and cannot judge baseline. The person who can is the aide, who sees the patient every morning and says 'she's not herself today.' Nobody asks the aide.
solution: A structured, plain-language daily check on a phone, with a voice option in the aide's language. It records a few observations against the patient's own baseline: gait, speech, new headache behavior, appetite, alertness and a free-text 'not herself'. A protocol turns 'change from baseline' into three levels: log, call the nurse today, or send to the ED. Alerts land in the clinic's inbox with a timeline. Aides get a small per-check stipend. The agency gets a revenue share. The practice gets documentation for safety programs and the patient-family peace of mind that keeps them on therapy.
why_now: The FDA approved Leqembi Iqlik, a home-administered subcutaneous starting dose, in July 2026, with launch in late August. Fewer infusion visits means fewer clinician touchpoints, while MRI-based ARIA monitoring remains. FDA-cleared blood tests are increasing the number of treated patients. CMS finalized new 2026 remote-monitoring codes for 2-15 days of data (99445) and the first 10 minutes of management (99470), making light-touch programs billable. Self-reported observations alone do not qualify for RPM, so the model pairs with a connected BP or pulse-ox device or bills through care-management routes such as CCM, PCM or GUIDE.
revenue_model: $45-65 per patient per month paid by the practice. A $10-15 per month stipend to the aide or agency comes out of that. Optional device add-on to unlock RPM billing. Later, pharma-funded real-world safety and function studies drawn from the aide-observed baseline data.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clinical sensor for a patient who cannot self-report is the person who changes their sheets. Aide phrasing like 'not herself' or 'slower' is a better early signal than a symptom checklist the patient can't complete, and it arrives as a behavior change, not a complaint. Home care agencies have always been treated as a cost center by clinics. Here they become a data channel that clinics will pay for.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 memory clinic nurse coordinators and two infusion-center managers and ask what they do between MRIs. Build the check as a no-login web form and SMS. Recruit 3 agencies whose clients are on Leqembi or Kisunla, plus a neurologist champion. Offer a free 90-day pilot on 15 patients, with a monthly report of flags raised and calls avoided. Convert to per-patient pricing once one true early catch is documented.

title: Identical Object Kits for Robot Data Farms
one_liner: Manufacture and ship standardized kits of hundreds of everyday-object variants, panels of handles, hinges and knobs, and task fixtures, so that every home and lab collecting robot training data uses the same physical objects.
customer: Robot-learning startups and university labs, and the data-collection vendors that run gig-worker networks who record household demonstrations for humanoid and manipulation models.
problem: At-home robot data collection is booming, but contributors use whatever cups, jars and cabinet handles they own. That makes data hard to compare, hard to control for variation and impossible to replicate across sites. A robot learning to open a drawer needs the same drawer types in 500 places.
solution: A 'Kitchen-100' kit: 100 standardized, individually scanned objects (cups, lids, jars, tongs, utensils, packages), plus modular handle, hinge, latch and knob panels and drawer or door fixtures with known mass, friction and geometry. Ship to thousands of contributors and to labs. Sell new object sets monthly so datasets keep growing coherently, and bundle the digital twins (scans and physics parameters) for simulation.
why_now: Humanoid and robot-foundation-model companies are competing for training data in 2026, and coverage such as MIT Technology Review's April 2026 report on gig workers training humanoids at home shows the supply chain for that data is still improvised. Only a handful of vendors can collect at scale, and none owns the standardized physical layer.
revenue_model: Kit sales ($150 to $600 each in batches of hundreds or thousands), monthly new-object subscriptions, custom fixture builds for labs ($5k to $50k) and licensing of scan and physics data.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for physical AI is not only more demonstrations but controlled, comparable ones. Whoever ships the same 100 objects to 5,000 kitchens gets a natural experiment in robot learning, and the kit sets the de facto benchmark. Old benchmarks (like a single reference set of household objects) are small and dated, so a manufacturing-scale, refreshable standard can become infrastructure.
first_30_days: Design and print or source a v0 kit of 50 to 100 objects and a set of handle panels. Scan each object and publish a free open dataset as marketing. Pitch 15 labs and 5 data-collection vendors with a pilot offer: 20 kits at cost plus a custom object of their choice. Target one vendor pilot of 200 kits.

title: Contingency Recovery of Unpaid Implant Carve-Outs
one_liner: Find and collect the implant and device carve-out payments that hospitals and surgery centers are owed but never bill, because the invoice lives in accounts payable and not in the billing office.
customer: Physician-owned spine and orthopedic ASCs, plus small and mid-size hospital ortho/spine/cardiac service lines, with commercial payer contracts that carve out implants. Paid 20-30% of recovered dollars.
problem: Many commercial contracts pay implants and high-cost devices separately, at invoice cost plus a markup, but only if the vendor invoice is submitted with the claim. The implant log is in the OR record, the invoice is in supply chain or AP, and the claim is built by billing. Nobody connects them. The claim goes out with L8699 or revenue code 027x lines at billed charges, and the payer pays $0 for the device or folds it into the case rate. The payment posts as 'paid', so nobody notices the loss. This is $5k-$50k per case for spine and joint work.
solution: Ingest the implant log (manufacturer, catalog and lot numbers), AP invoice PDFs (parsed with an LLM), contract carve-out terms extracted from the PDFs, and the 837/835 files. Compute expected carve-out payment versus actual, auto-assemble invoice attachments per payer rules, and file corrected claims and appeals inside timely-filing windows. Run it as a service for the first clients (manual, coder-led), then automate the matching.
why_now: CMS's CY2026 outpatient rule began phasing out the inpatient-only list and added many procedures, mostly musculoskeletal, to the ASC-covered list. More device-heavy spine and ortho cases are moving to ASCs whose small billing staffs have never dealt with carve-outs. Payers are also using AI-driven payment integrity that makes missing attachments an automatic zero.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered carve-out payments. After the first recovery, convert to $1.5-4k/month prospective monitoring per facility.
non_obvious_insight: The loss is invisible in every standard revenue-cycle KPI. Denial rate looks fine and AR looks fine because the line paid 'as billed under the case rate'. The only way to see it is to lay the supply chain invoice next to the contract term next to the 835. Billers know it happens. Supply chain does not know payers pay for it. Finance never audits it. That gap between three departments is the earned secret.
first_30_days: Pick 10 physician-owned spine and ortho ASCs through ASCA chapters and surgeon-owner LinkedIn outreach. Offer a free 90-day lookback audit, since contingency means zero risk to them. Each needs to share 835s, implant logs, invoices and the top three commercial contracts. Do the first three audits by hand with a coder and a spreadsheet, and use the dollars found as the sales collateral. Then automate the invoice parsing.

title: Home-Readiness Crews for Hospital-at-Home Programs
one_liner: On-call crews that make a patient's home hospital-ready in hours and provide a non-clinical overnight presence for the first 72 hours.
customer: Hospital-at-Home program directors at health systems, and Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs that fund them.
problem: Extending the waiver lets programs scale, but many referred patients get screened out because of clutter, stairs, pets, bad Wi-Fi or power, no bedside space, or no adult present overnight. Every screen-out is a lost admission that would have replaced $2,500+ inpatient days. No one owns the home itself.
solution: A van and two-person crew does a rapid home assessment (power, connectivity via hotspot or eSIM, safe path, bedside setup, hazard removal, DME handoff). A vetted sitter provides overnight presence and escalates to the nurse line, and the crew resets the home at discharge. An address-based readiness score pre-screens referrals before the ED sends them.
why_now: The Hospital-at-Home waiver was extended five years, to Sep 30, 2030, so systems are committing capital and hiring. 80+ growth and 90% occupancy in senior housing mean more frail patients whose homes are the constraint.
revenue_model: Per-episode fee of $350-900 plus monthly retainers for guaranteed response, and a software license for the readiness score.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource isn't clinicians or tech; it's a safe physical environment and a body in the room at 3 am. Whoever solves 'make the home hospital-grade' raises hospital-at-home conversion rates, which is what programs are judged on.
first_30_days: Pitch three hospital-at-home directors and offer a pilot at cost on 20 episodes, using existing local caregiver and sitter pools. Track screen-out conversion and cost per episode.

title: Alt-Data From AI-Training Gig Workers
one_liner: A worker-owned pay-transparency panel for expert data contractors. Its aggregated signals on which domains are hiring, what they pay and how many hours exist become a leading-indicator dataset for investors and rival platforms.
customer: Hedge funds, VCs and AI-lab competitive-intelligence teams pay $30-150k a year for the index. Workers get the basic tier free or for $9-15 a month.
problem: Mercor's reported gross run rate went from about $0.5B to $2B in nine months, and the category claims millions of contractors, yet nobody outside the labs can see which skills are in demand or when a domain saturates. Workers complain of falling pay and have no rate data, while investors price a $10-25B category on anecdotes.
solution: A browser extension plus web app where contractors log, or auto-capture from their own dashboards, pay rate, hours offered, rejections and coarse project category (never confidential content). There is a public 'Levels.fyi for AI gigs' leaderboard by platform and domain, and a paid weekly index of hours availability and pay by domain, with saturation early-warnings.
why_now: The human-data market went from niche to multi-billion in a year, contractors are publicly vocal (HN, Verge, Wired coverage) and investor appetite for AI-adjacent labor data is high. No panel exists.
revenue_model: Institutional data subscriptions ($50-150k a year), a premium worker tier ($9-15 a month) and possibly sponsored placements from challenger platforms recruiting supply.
non_obvious_insight: Gig workers are usually treated as supply, but here they are a sensor network that reads the frontier labs' priorities weeks before any press release. Workers will join because it helps them negotiate and avoid saturated domains. Platforms can't easily object to workers sharing their own pay data, provided the design avoids NDA-covered project details.
first_30_days: Seed 300 members from data-annotation subreddits and Discords with a pay-rate survey. Publish a 'State of expert AI gig pay' report. Pitch 10 funds and 3 VC platform teams a sample weekly index, and land one paid pilot.

title: Displaced Insurance Agents Become Rooftop Solar Navigators
one_liner: Recruit the micro-agents wiped out by India's proposed insurance commission cuts as the trust-and-paperwork channel for rooftop solar, batteries and induction retrofits, paid per install by installers and lenders.
customer: MNRE-empanelled EPC installers and lenders (PSU banks, NBFCs) who pay per verified install or disbursed loan. The micro-agents (POSPs, motor-insurance agents, CSC operators) are the supply side.
problem: IRDAI's 2026-09-23 draft cuts general-insurance commission caps from 30% to 20%, sets 0% on motor third-party and 5% on own-damage, and PB Fintech fell 36% in one day. Hundreds of thousands of small agents in tier-2 and tier-3 towns lose most of their income. Meanwhile household solar and electrification demand is throttled by last-mile trust and paperwork (DISCOM feasibility, net-metering, subsidy claims, loans) rather than by hardware cost.
solution: A navigator app with training and payout rails. The agent walks a household through eligibility, vendor selection, DISCOM application, subsidy claim, bank loan and insurance for the new asset, earning per completed milestone. The annual motor-renewal touchpoint becomes the sales moment, and battery and induction bundles are added. The platform handles KYC, lead routing, quality control and payouts.
why_now: The IRDAI draft is days old and distributors such as PolicyBazaar and Turtlemint are squeezed and looking for new products. India's government-backed rooftop programs (verify current PM Surya Ghar terms) and LPG-shock induction demand are pulling households toward electrification, and UPI makes micro-payouts cheap.
revenue_model: INR 3,000-6,000 per installed home from the EPC (about 2-4% of net system cost), INR 1,000-2,000 per loan from lenders, insurance attach for the new asset, with the platform keeping 20-30% of bounties.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation just stranded a trusted, KYC'd, paperwork-fluent field force at the exact moment the bottleneck in electrification moved from hardware cost to last-mile trust. Insurance micro-agents are a distribution network searching for a product, and rooftop solar is a product searching for distribution.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 agents in one district through motor-insurance agent WhatsApp and Telegram communities and CSC networks. Sign 2 local EPCs on a per-commissioned-install bounty, run 20 installs end to end, and measure conversion from renewal touchpoints. Pay agents by UPI after commissioning.

title: Compliant Format Kit for Card-Break Sellers
one_liner: Counsel-designed formats and software that let breakers, repackers and game stores run randomized break and mystery-pack sales without tripping lottery law.
customer: Independent breakers and repack sellers on Whatnot, eBay and TikTok, plus game stores that run break nights.
problem: Random spot-assignment breaks are being attacked as illegal lotteries under California Penal Code 319. Fifteen arbitration demands were filed in March 2026 for 30+ clients (about 100 expected). A July 2025 suit names Whatnot and Fanatics Live, and a qui tam action was recently unsealed. Independent sellers carry exposure with no counsel and no tooling.
solution: Alternative formats (pick-your-own-team, guaranteed-value floors, no-purchase-necessary entry flows), a per-state rule engine with registration and bonding reminders, an audit-logged randomizer with retained video, age and spend-limit controls, odds-disclosure templates, and dispute-ready records.
why_now: Arbitrations run 12-18 months, so seller uncertainty peaks through 2027. Platforms are defending, not building seller tooling.
revenue_model: $79-299/month SaaS by seller volume, a legal-review add-on, compliance audits, and licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation targets platforms, but the marginal legal risk sits with small sellers whose margins cannot absorb it. Nobody sells them a compliant product design, and the fix is to change the product (make assignment non-random or value-guaranteed), which software can standardize. Whether breaks are illegal is unsettled, so retain gaming counsel.
first_30_days: Retain consumer-gaming counsel. Publish a free state-by-state cheat sheet. Recruit 20 mid-size breakers through Discords and pilot a pick-your-spot format with a guaranteed floor at $99/month.
